title: Zoning-rule review register: a permanent, structured record of every implemented zoning rule (law link, where it applies, plain-English interpretation, worked example, code and tests, revision, a human verdict only a named reviewer can set), with a short current table, detail pages, an append-only history, a build-time check and a backfill of the 23 rule files (D-090-R362..R385)
objective: Create the permanent zoning-rule review register the owner asked for on 2026-10-06 (D-090 source-042): a record the owner can hand to a New York City architect or examiner that shows, for each zoning rule the program implements, the law it rests on, where it applies and its exceptions, the program's interpretation in plain English, one concrete example (inputs, the expected answer, the answer the program actually gives), the code and tests, its revision, and a HUMAN verdict field that only a named human reviewer's own answer may fill. Build it the way the rule-coverage matrix is built (services/api/app/rules/coverage/: authored JSON, a deterministic renderer, a test that the committed Markdown equals the renderer's output): one structured data file with stable ids and fixed field names (so it can move into a database table later; NO database work now), rendered to a short current table, one detail page per rule and an append-only history. Backfill every rule file under services/api/app/rules/rulesets/ (23 today) from evidence that can be checked - the rule file, the captured law text under docs/research/zr-snapshots/v1/, the tests - and mark every gap as a gap. Add a test in the api suite that fails when a rule file changes without the register being updated, so the standing instruction is enforced by the build and not by memory. Reuse the existing rule ids and evidence; point to the coverage matrix, the captures and docs/ARCHITECT_REVIEW_QUESTIONS.md instead of copying them. This is a review record, not a gate: nothing may be made to wait for a verdict.
business_reason: Owner message 93 (D-090 source-042), rows R362 to R385: a permanent register for a later architect or examiner review; a separate Markdown file with a simple table; existing rule ids and evidence reused; eight named fields; automated test results kept apart from the human verdict; no rule ever marked professionally reviewed because tests or another AI passed it; a verdict bound to the version and conditions reviewed; a short current table with linked details and an append-only history; old records preserved and affected reviews flagged when a rule changes; no duplicate entries; a short standing instruction in the main instruction file; the detail not loaded into every session; a backfill from verifiable evidence with gaps marked; not a new mandatory sign-off stage; stable ids and structured fields; no database integration now.

acceptance_scenarios.input: docs/zoning-rule-review/REGISTER.md and one detail page, read without the code
acceptance_scenarios.expected: REGISTER.md is a short table with one row per rule: entry id, rule title, law section with its official link and applicable date, revision and date last changed, automated-test status, human verdict, reviewer and date, and a link to the detail page. A detail page shows, in plain English, where the rule applies and its exceptions, the program's interpretation, the example (inputs, expected answer with its basis, actual program answer), links to the code and tests, the evidence (capture id, digest, capture date), the gaps, and the human review block. An architect can follow it without opening the repository's code

every field of the owner's list is present under a fixed name: rule id and official law link with applicable date; where it applies and exceptions; interpretation; example (inputs, expected, actual); code and test links; revision and date last changed; human verdict with exactly the four values 'Not reviewed', 'Correct', 'Incorrect', 'Needs re-review'; reviewer name, date and comments. Automated-test status is a SEPARATE field from the human verdict. entry_id equals the existing rule_id and never changes. GUIDE.md lists the field names and value sets; no database file exists

the test asserts a one-to-one match between rule files and register entries (23 today; no entry without a rule file, no rule file without an entry, no duplicate id), and that every linked code file, test file and capture file exists

acceptance_scenarios.input: a rule file whose rule_version or content differs from what the entry records
acceptance_scenarios.expected: each entry records the rule file's rule_version and a line-ending-normalized sha256 of the rule file; the test fails with a message that names the rule and says the register must be updated in the same change (new revision, history event). MUTATION PROOF in the producer report: edit one rule file in a scratch copy, show the test red, restore

the test evaluates every example's inputs through the program's own rule registry and evaluator and asserts the result equals the 'actual' recorded in the register; a recorded 'expected' never comes from a program run: it is either worked from the captured law text with the arithmetic shown, or taken from a named reference case, or marked as a gap. Where expected and actual differ, the entry says so plainly (a 'differs' flag) and is not hidden; the test does not force them equal

acceptance_scenarios.input: the human review block of every entry
acceptance_scenarios.expected: all 23 backfilled entries read 'Not reviewed' with empty reviewer fields. The checker REFUSES a verdict other than 'Not reviewed' without a reviewer name, a review date and the revision and conditions reviewed; it refuses 'Correct' or 'Incorrect' when the reviewed revision is not the entry's current revision (it must read 'Needs re-review'). Negative tests prove each refusal. Nothing derives a verdict from test status or from an AI review

every entry has a 'created' event for revision 1; event sequence numbers are contiguous from 1 and in date order; the current revision of each entry equals its latest event's revision; no two consecutive events of one entry are identical in what they record. GUIDE.md states that events are only added, and that a change of interpretation, applicability or implementation adds a new revision, keeps the old detail in the history and sets affected human verdicts to 'Needs re-review'. The limit is stated honestly: the test cannot see earlier commits, so a reviewer checks that a change only appends
the test renders from register.json and asserts byte-identical files on disk (line endings normalized), as test_coverage_matrix.py does for the coverage matrix; no stale or orphan detail page

a missing independent example, a law section read but not captured, a rule with no test of its own, an exception the rule file names but does not compute, a special-district interaction that is a stub: each is written in the entry's gaps list in plain words. No field holds an invented value; no example copies a number from the owner's sample report. Every entry carries the standing note that the rule is an unreviewed draft

acceptance_scenarios.input: modules that apply zoning law without a rule id (for example the wide-street wiring and the named-street override table under services/api/app/rules/, and zoning arithmetic in the scenario engine)
acceptance_scenarios.expected: REPORTED in the producer report and listed in GUIDE.md under a heading that says these are not yet in the register and why; NOT given invented rule ids and NOT changed. The orchestrator turns the list into follow-up work

only allowed_paths changed; no rule file, engine, registry, snapshot, coverage, CI, dependency or database file changed; no gate, task or check is made to depend on a human verdict; the full services/api pytest and ruff pass

acceptance_scenarios.input: an entry with a recorded human decision, then a change to the rule file, to a cited law capture, or to the entry's interpretation, applicability or example
acceptance_scenarios.expected: the human review block keeps the reviewer's ORIGINAL decision exactly as given (decision, reviewer name and role, date, comments, the revision reviewed, the conditions reviewed) together with the identity of what was reviewed: the rule file's digest, the digests of the cited law captures and the entry's revision. A SEPARATE field says whether that decision applies to the current version; it is DERIVED by comparing those recorded identities with the current ones, never typed. The verdict shown in the table follows from the two: no decision -> 'Not reviewed'; a decision whose identities all match -> that decision; a decision whose identities do not all match -> 'Needs re-review', with the earlier decision still shown as 'earlier decision: Correct, given for revision N'. Tests prove: (a) a rule file changes under a 'Correct' decision and the register's recorded rule digest is updated in the same change -> the entry reads 'Needs re-review' and the original decision is still there; (b) merely updating or touching the register file cannot make an old 'Correct' apply to changed logic - the checker refuses a shown verdict of 'Correct' when any reviewed identity differs from the current one; (c) the same for a changed law capture digest; (d) a history event records the decision and a later event records that it no longer applies

acceptance_scenarios.input: a rule change whose register entry is updated, with no human decision at all, and one with a decision that no longer applies
acceptance_scenarios.expected: the build check passes in both cases: it requires only that the record is current (the entry's recorded identities match the files, a new revision and a history event exist). No check, test, gate or script requires a human decision, and none fails because an entry reads 'Not reviewed' or 'Needs re-review'. A test asserts exactly that, and GUIDE.md says it in one plain sentence

acceptance_scenarios.input: each entry's description of what the rule does
acceptance_scenarios.expected: each detail page separates three lists in plain words: what the committed rule computes AND a named test exercises (with the test's name); what the committed rule contains that no test exercises; what is planned or not built (today's gaps that are missing behaviour). Nothing planned is described as existing. The lists are built by reading the rule file and its test file, not from memory; where it cannot be told whether a behaviour is exercised, the entry says so

acceptance_scenarios.input: the automated-tests field of every entry and the table's test column
acceptance_scenarios.expected: the field holds a RESULT, not a count: status 'Passed', 'Failed' or 'Not run'; the exact commit the tests were run at; the date; the command; and a link to the evidence of that run (a committed log of the run under docs/zoning-rule-review/evidence/, with the counts). The result is bound to the identity of what was tested (the rule file's digest and the digests of the test files): the checker requires the shown status to be 'Not run' when any of them differs from the current files, so a result for an earlier version is never shown as current. The table column shows the status and the short commit, never 'N test files'. The test result stays a separate field from the human review block, and nothing derives one from the other

acceptance_scenarios.input: REGISTER.md, GUIDE.md and the entries named in the first review's notes
acceptance_scenarios.expected: the introduction says the register covers the 23 rule-definition files the program has today and that this is not complete coverage of the law; agent reviews are called agent reviews and nothing reads as a human or professional review; the five notes of the first independent review are applied: F1 (r5a-height basis wording), F2 (r5b-height and r5d-height: the statement-to-district mapping named as a gap), F3 (the misnamed test strengthened to run the checker on a tampered copy), F4 (the append-only limit stated as a standing duty of each reviewer), F5 (r2x-r4-residential-far: 'R4 1.50; R2X unchanged at 1.00')

risks: An 'expected answer' copied from the program's own output would make the register circular -> S5: expected comes from the law text, a reference case, or is a gap
A register that silently goes stale is worse than none -> S4 and S8 make the build fail
A human verdict written by a session -> S6: refused without a named reviewer, a date and the revision reviewed; all backfilled rows read 'Not reviewed'
Scope creep into rule fixes: the backfill will surface doubts about rules -> they are written as gaps and reported, never fixed here

The plain-English interpretation could overstate what a draft rule covers -> every row carries the unreviewed-draft note and its limits; an independent reviewer re-derives the examples from the captured text
The standing instruction must fit under the 10,000-token cap on automatically loaded instructions -> one or two lines, added by the orchestrator after the open instruction change (PR #448) merges
